newsitem.title: INDIA: India banks shrug off ICICI lending cut.
newsitem.headline: India banks shrug off ICICI lending cut.

text.p: A new short-term lending rate announced by the Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India Ltd (ICICI), though lower than normal banking rates, is unlikely to lead to any cut in banks' lending rates, bankers and analysts said on Friday.
ICICI is India's second largest term lending bank.
ICICI said effective July 24, its short-term prime lending rate would be 12.50 percent per annum. The lowest prime lending rate charged by Indian banks is 13.5 percent.
Until now, ICICI had only two rates, one for long term and the other for medium term loans.
"There is no immediate reason for us to cut rates," a top official of public sector Canara Bank said.

"ICICI is not a major competitor for us in the market for working capital loans," he said. "Our decision on interest rates will be taken more based on our analysis of cost of funds and demand and supply of funds," he said.
A top official at the private HDFC Bank agreed.

"I do not think that banks will cut rates just because ICICI has cut rates. If you look at the past, when ICICI set a MTPR (medium term lending rate) of 13 pct against bank prime rates of 13.5 percent, there was no reaction from banks."
The Industrial Development Bank (IDBI), India's top term lending bank, said its focus would continue to be on long-term finance.
"This may be a short-term response to a temporary surplus with the institution," an IDBI official said about ICICI's decision to offer short-term loans at 12.5 percent a year.
The IDBI official said recent trends in demand for credit were encouraging and indicated that demand could pick up in the second half of 1997/98 (April-March).
Banking analysts said the impact of ICICI's decision will be minimal.
"They are earmarking about 35 percent of their loans for short tenure," said an analyst with a European brokerage.
He said ICICI was targeting 130 billion rupees of total loans this year. "They will rope in some of their existing long term borrowers. But it won't eat into bank loans market."
